row.Name: Zimmie Reva Shelton
row.College connection: Graduated from Spelman College in 1929.
row.Institutional Connection and Legacy:
Taught art in Atlanta public schools for approximately fifty years.
Saved money from her Social Security payments for her grandchildren’s education. Helped her grandson, filmmaker Shelton Jackson “Spike” Lee, attend Morehouse College and New York University.
Provided early funding for Lee’s first feature film, She’s Gotta Have It.
Married postal employee Richard Jackson Shelton, who died in 1976.
Spelman College records also identify her as Zimmie Retha Shelton.

row.Name: Jewel Woodward Simon
row.College connection: Graduated summa cum laude from Atlanta University.
row.Institutional Connection and Legacy:
Earned her undergraduate degree, summa cum laude, from Atlanta University.
Studied painting with Hale Woodruff and sculpture with Alice Dunbar.
Became the first Black graduate awarded a bachelor of fine arts degree by the Atlanta School of Art in 1967.
Her Atlanta University degree is dated 1930 by the Texas State Historical Association and 1931 by the biographical directory reproduced by Prabook.
row.Biography:
Taught mathematics at Jack Yates High School in Houston before settling in Atlanta with her husband, Edward Lloyd Simon.
Worked in painting, sculpture and printmaking, alongside interests in music and poetry.
Helped found the National Conference of Negro Artists and participated in Atlanta’s civic arts leadership.
row.Sources:
D. L. Henderson: South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), pp. 241-242

row.Name: Louie Delphia Davis Shivery
row.College connection: Earned a master?s degree from Atlanta University in 1936.
row.Institutional Connection and Legacy: Earned a master’s degree at Atlanta University. Her 1936 thesis examined organized social work among Black Atlantans from 1890 to 1935.
row.Biography:
Headed the English department at Booker T. Washington High School and wrote the school’s song.
Helped develop Atlanta’s Neighborhood Union and served as its executive secretary and historian.
Contributed to the Atlanta Daily World and served as president of the Atlanta Metropolitan Council of Negro Women.
Served on the board of the Colored Branch of the Atlanta Tuberculosis Association.
row.Sources:
D. L. Henderson: South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), p. 241

row.Name: Nellie Harriet Watts
row.College connection: Graduated from Atlanta University in 1910.
row.Institutional Connection and Legacy: Graduated from Atlanta University?s college course in 1910 and continued her education at Detroit Teachers College.
row.Biography:
Taught in Detroit public schools and organized concert presentations featuring Black performers.
Used her own funds to bring Marian Anderson to Detroit for her first performance in the city in 1937.
Presented the Nellie Watts Concert Series for twenty-five years. Its artists included Leontyne Price, Paul Robeson and the Alvin Ailey Dance Theatre.
Founded an arts-support organization in Detroit and served on the Detroit NAACP board.
Was a daughter of South-View Cemetery co-founder Albert Watts.
row.Sources:
D. L. Henderson: South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), p. 249
Detroit Historical Society: program documenting 1971 presentation of Watts portrait | https://www.detroithistorical.org/learn/online-research/collection/archive/program-193

row.Name: Wilmere Kathleen Redding Adams
row.College connection: Completed Atlanta University?s high school and normal teacher-training course in 1911.
row.Institutional Connection and Legacy:
Grew up on Auburn Avenue as the daughter of Wesley Chapel Redding and Ellen Redding.
Preserved local history through oral histories and her work as historian of First Congregational Church.
Served on the Auburn Avenue Research Library’s board and became known for her knowledge of Atlanta’s Black community.
Her death year differs between sources: Atlanta History Center’s authority record gives 1993, while Henderson’s South-View book lists 2003.

row.Name: Julia Agnes Washington Bond
row.College connection: Earned a master?s degree in library science from Atlanta University and worked in its libraries until retiring in 2000.
row.Institutional Connection and Legacy:
Returned to school at age fifty-six and earned a master’s degree in library science from Atlanta University.
Worked at Atlanta University’s Trevor Arnett Library and later as a part-time reference librarian at Robert W. Woodruff Library.
Retired from library work in 2000 at age ninety-two.
row.Biography:
Attended Fisk University in Nashville, where she met educator Horace Mann Bond.
Supported her children’s civil rights work, including the organizing and public service of her son Julian Bond.
row.Sources:
D. L. Henderson: South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), p. 177
The HistoryMakers: Julia Bond oral-history biography | https://www.thehistorymakers.org/biography/julia-bond-41

portrait_status: Archival lead: video oral history; portrait file not obtained
notes: Do not repeat HistoryMakers errors identifying Horace as AU president and death 1973. Book identifies him as dean and dates death 1972. Degree year unverified.
timeline_basis: 2000 is documented library retirement, not graduation year.

row.Name: Minnie Dyer
row.College connection: Graduated from Morris Brown College.
row.Institutional Connection and Legacy:
Graduated from Morris Brown College and Atlanta University before earning her teaching credentials.
Began temporary teaching work in Atlanta public schools in 1910 and joined Mitchell Street School full time in 1911.
Taught at Ashby Street School and, after retiring from public schools, at Our Lady of Lourdes Catholic School.
row.Biography:
Worked as a seamstress before entering teaching.
Taught her niece Pearlie Craft Dove, who later became a noted educator at Clark College.
Was a daughter of Caleb and Emma Dyer. Her father, a carpenter, purchased the family’s first cemetery land at South-View.
row.Sources: D. L. Henderson: South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), pp. 36-38

portrait_status: Found in book: identified group photo, printed p.37
notes: Book-based biography; no reliable additional online biography found. Minnie Lee Dyer (1916–1999), buried in Durham, is a different person and excluded. Book photo identifies Minnie standing at far right, credit Carol Dove; needs extraction and portrait preparation.

row.Name: Harold Irvin Bearden
row.College connection: Graduated from Morris Brown College and Turner Theological Seminary. Served as chair of Morris Brown?s board of trustees, a role documented in 1977.
row.Institutional Connection and Legacy:
Graduated from Morris Brown College and Turner Theological Seminary.
Chaired Morris Brown?s board of trustees and helped the college work toward accreditation.
Was identified as Morris Brown?s board chair in a report published February 4, 1977.
row.Biography:
Became pastor of Big Bethel AME Church in Atlanta in 1951.
Used radio sermons to speak against segregation and participated in civil rights protests.
Served as president of the Atlanta NAACP.
Was elected a bishop of the African Methodist Episcopal Church in 1964.

D. L. Henderson: South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), p. 173

row.Name: Fred C. Bennette Jr.
row.College connection: Attended Morris Brown College and Turner Theological Seminary. Helped organize the 1960 sit-in campaign while a Morris Brown student.
row.Institutional Connection and Legacy:
Attended Morris Brown College and Turner Theological Seminary.
Helped organize the 1960 campaign against segregation at Rich’s department store while a Morris Brown student.
row.Biography:
Served in the U.S. Army before returning to Atlanta for further education and civil rights work.
Organized voter-registration campaigns and worked closely with Martin Luther King Jr. and Andrew Young.
Became the first director of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference’s Operation Breadbasket, which challenged discriminatory employment practices.
Later advised Jimmy Carter and Andrew Young and served the King Center as an adviser and security director.
row.Sources:
D. L. Henderson: South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), p. 174

row.Name: Hilliard D. Canady
row.College connection: Attended Morris Brown College and Turner Theological Seminary.
row.Institutional Connection and Legacy: Attended Morris Brown College and Turner Theological Seminary. Also studied at Meharry Medical College.
row.Biography:
Was born in Troup County, Georgia, in 1859 and served as a presiding elder in the African Methodist Episcopal Church.
Married Nora Lee Bryant Canady, a Clark College graduate and church worker.
Their son, Hilliard D. Canady Jr., became a physician and medical inspector of Atlanta’s Black public schools. Father and son died in 1932.
row.Sources: D. L. Henderson: South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), p. 185

notes: Book-based profile; no reliable additional online biography or identified portrait found for elder Canady. Do not assign physician/football-coach son's achievements to father.

row.Name: William Alfred Fountain Sr.
row.College connection: Graduated from Morris Brown College and served as its fifth president from 1911 to 1920. Later served as chancellor.
row.Institutional Connection and Legacy:
Earned degrees from Morris Brown College and Turner Theological Seminary.
Served as Morris Brown’s fifth president from 1911 to 1920 and later as chancellor.
Worked alongside his son, William Alfred Fountain Jr., to sustain the college during financial hardship.
Fountain Hall, formerly Atlanta University’s Stone Hall, bears his name.
row.Biography:
Served as an African Methodist Episcopal minister and became a bishop in 1920.
Led congregations and worked to improve their buildings and finances.
Participated in civic organizations and supported Black higher education.
row.Sources:
D. L. Henderson: South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), p. 200
National Park Service: Atlanta University Center historic district nomination | https://npgallery.nps.gov/NRHP/GetAsset/1b062e51-9356-4645-a747-d87a5d6e6237/

row.Name: William Alfred Fountain Jr.
row.College connection: Served as Morris Brown College?s seventh president from 1929 to 1950.
row.Institutional Connection and Legacy:
Served as Morris Brown College’s seventh president from 1929 to 1950.
Led the college through the Great Depression with support from his father, William Alfred Fountain Sr., who served as chancellor.
Chose to take no salary during the financial crisis while Morris Brown reorganized to remain open.
During his administration, Morris Brown joined the Atlanta University Center and relocated to the former Atlanta University campus.
row.Biography: After leaving Morris Brown, served as secretary-treasurer of the African Methodist Episcopal Church’s General Board of Education.
row.Sources:
D. L. Henderson: South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), p. 200
National Park Service: Atlanta University Center historic district nomination | https://npgallery.nps.gov/NRHP/GetAsset/1b062e51-9356-4645-a747-d87a5d6e6237/

row.Name: Evelyn Jones Frazier
row.College connection: Graduated from Morris Brown College in 1952.
row.Institutional Connection and Legacy: Earned a bachelor’s degree from Morris Brown College in 1952 while developing her restaurant business.
row.Biography:
Opened the Evelyn Jones Cafe in 1936. Expanded the business with her husband, Luther Ellis Frazier, in the 1940s as Frazier’s Cafe Society.
Provided a meeting place for Black civic, religious and civil rights organizations. Patrons included Benjamin Mays, Martin Luther King Jr. and Thurgood Marshall.
Supported businesswomen’s organizations and the NAACP.
row.Sources:
D. L. Henderson: South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), p. 201

row.Name: Cornelius King
row.College connection: Served as a trustee of Morris Brown College.
row.Institutional Connection and Legacy: Served as a trustee of Morris Brown College.
row.Biography:
Worked in Atlanta’s private clubs and later in Washington, D.C., before establishing businesses serving Black Atlantans.
Opened King’s Wigwam, a recreation resort near Kennesaw, in 1918.
Helped organize Mercy Hospital in 1919 and served as its superintendent.
Founded Cornelius King & Son real estate in 1922. His son Turner later headed the family firm.
Chaired Big Bethel AME Church’s trustees. His second wife, Nina Culver King, was a Spelman graduate.
row.Sources:
D. L. Henderson: South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), pp. 219-220

row.Name: John Henry Lewis
row.College connection: Graduated from Morris Brown College in 1905. Served as its president from 1920 to 1928 and again from 1951 to 1958.
row.Institutional Connection and Legacy:
Graduated from Morris Brown College in 1905 and later joined its faculty.
Served as the college’s sixth president from 1920 to 1928.
Returned as its eighth president in 1951 and remained in office until his death in 1958.
row.Biography:
Studied ministry at Yale Divinity School and pursued graduate education at the University of Chicago.
Served as an African Methodist Episcopal minister and educational administrator in several states.
Led Dunbar High School and Shorter College and served as dean of Payne Theological Seminary.
Was the father of historian David Levering Lewis.
row.Sources:
D. L. Henderson: South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), p. 222
Yale University Library: John Henry Lewis biography and portrait | https://onlineexhibits.library.yale.edu/s/early-black-yale-students/item/20972

portrait_status: Found: downloaded and visually checked Yale portrait

row.Name: John Wesley Edward Linder
row.College connection: Graduated from Morris Brown College.
row.Institutional Connection and Legacy: Graduated from Morris Brown College and continued his medical education at Meharry Medical College.
row.Biography:
Began practicing medicine in Dublin, Georgia, before relocating to Atlanta.
Served as president of the Atlanta Medical Association and Georgia Medical Association, professional organizations for Black physicians.
Established the Georgia Medical Association’s first quarterly journal.
Served on the National Medical Association’s executive board.
row.Sources: D. L. Henderson: South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), p. 223

notes: Book-based profile; no reliable additional online biography or identified portrait found. Omit book's unverified characterization of father George W. Linder as congressman; confirm office first.

row.Name: Henry James Charles Bowden
row.College connection: Graduated from Morehouse College in 1925.
row.Institutional Connection and Legacy:
Graduated from Morehouse College in 1925.
Continued his education at General Theological Seminary and Columbia University.
row.Biography:
Was ordained an Episcopal priest in 1929 and became rector of St. Paul’s Episcopal Church in Atlanta in 1934.
Served as a military and Veterans Administration chaplain.
Worked with aging-service organizations and the NAACP, advocating for older adults.
Fulton County’s H. J. C. Bowden senior multipurpose facility was named in recognition of his work.
row.Sources:
D. L. Henderson: South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), p. 178

row.Name: Clifford Nathaniel Ellis
row.College connection: Graduated from Morehouse College in 1926 and its School of Religion in 1927.
row.Institutional Connection and Legacy:
Completed Morehouse Academy before graduating from Morehouse College in 1926.
Earned a divinity degree from the Morehouse School of Religion in 1927.
row.Biography:
Pastored churches in Georgia and led Reed Street, later Paradise, Baptist Church for more than four decades.
Extended the church’s reach through the Chariot Wheels gospel radio broadcast.
Served as president of the Atlanta Baptist Ministers Union and on the National Baptist Convention’s board.
Married Vashti Scott Ellis, a journalist in the Atlanta Daily World publishing family.
row.Sources:
D. L. Henderson: South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), p. 197

row.Name: Charles Walter Greenlea
row.College connection: Graduated from Morehouse College.
row.Institutional Connection and Legacy: Graduated from Morehouse College and earned a master’s degree from Atlanta University.
row.Biography:
Served for twenty years as executive director of the Atlanta NAACP.
Worked as an editor at the Atlanta Daily World and with Economic Opportunity Atlanta.
Co-founded and led Summerhill Neighborhood Inc., working on housing and neighborhood development.
Greenlea Commons in Summerhill was named in his honor.
row.Sources: D. L. Henderson: South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), p. 203

row.Name: Rogers Henderson
row.College connection: Was named an honorary alumnus of Morehouse College. With his wife, contributed a stained-glass window and painting to its Danforth Chapel.
row.Institutional Connection and Legacy:
Was named an honorary alumnus of Morehouse College in recognition of his support.
With his wife, contributed a stained-glass window and painting to Morehouse’s Danforth Chapel.
row.Biography:
Founded Henderson Realty Company on Auburn Avenue and helped establish the Empire Real Estate Board.
Worked with his wife, Ida Franklin Henderson, who joined the business and held leadership roles in Black women’s civic organizations.

D. L. Henderson: South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), p. 209

row.Name: Charles Dubois Hubert
row.College connection: Graduated from Morehouse College in 1909. Directed its School of Religion and served as acting president from 1937 to 1940.
row.Institutional Connection and Legacy:
Completed Morehouse Academy in 1905 and earned a bachelor’s degree from Morehouse College in 1909.
Taught church history and directed the college’s School of Religion.
Served as acting president from 1937 to 1940, between the administrations of Samuel Archer and Benjamin Mays.
row.Biography:
Earned a divinity degree from Rochester Theological Seminary in 1912.
Served as pastor of Providence Baptist Church while working in higher education.
row.Sources:
D. L. Henderson: South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), p. 214

row.Name: Dennis Taylor Hubert
row.College connection: Studied divinity at Morehouse College in 1930. Received a posthumous honorary degree from the college in 2025.
row.Institutional Connection and Legacy:
Was eighteen when a white mob killed him on the Crogman School playground in Atlanta on June 15, 1930.
Was the son of minister Gaddus Johnson Hubert and educator Pearl Parks Hubert, and a nephew of Morehouse leader Charles Dubois Hubert.
His family faced further attacks after his killing.
Morehouse’s 2025 commencement records identify him as Dennis O. Hubert.
row.Biography:

His family faced further attacks after his killing.
row.Sources:
D. L. Henderson: South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), p. 214
Morehouse College: 2025 commencement, Dennis Hubert biography | https://morehouse.edu/events/signature-events/commencement/2025

row.Name: Graham Washington Jackson
row.College connection: Attended Morehouse College.
row.Institutional Connection and Legacy:
Attended Morehouse College and Atlanta University.
Sources differ on his Morehouse attendance dates: a family account places it in 1922–1923, while the New Georgia Encyclopedia gives 1924.
row.Biography:
Performed on piano, organ and accordion and led music at Booker T. Washington High School.
Played at wartime fundraising events and performed for U.S. presidents.
Became widely known through a 1945 photograph showing him playing the accordion in mourning for Franklin Roosevelt.
Led jazz ensembles, worked in broadcasting and performed at Atlanta venues.
Was named Georgia’s official state musician by Governor Jimmy Carter.
row.Sources:

row.Name: Phoebe Lucille Fraser Burney Callier Hart
row.College connection: Graduated from Clark College in 1935. Served as its dean of women from 1943 to 1958.
row.Institutional Connection and Legacy:
Graduated from Clark College in 1935 and pursued religious-education study at Gammon Theological Seminary.
Worked in Morehouse College’s endowment office before becoming Clark’s dean of women.
Served as dean of women at Clark College from 1943 to 1958.
row.Biography:
Directed religious education for the southeastern region of the Congregational church.
Later known as Phoebe Callier, served educational institutions in Chattanooga.
Sponsored two children from Africa and helped bring them to the United States.
row.Sources:
D. L. Henderson: South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), p. 208

row.Name: Cora B. Finley
row.College connection: Graduated from Spelman Seminary?s Academic Department in 1894.
row.Institutional Connection and Legacy:
Graduated from Spelman Seminary?s Academic Department in 1894 and became its first alumna to earn an advanced degree at Atlanta University.
Served as principal of Atlanta?s Yonge Street School and later led the education department at Alabama State University.
row.Biography:
Helped organize an early Black parent-teacher association in 1911.
Challenged unequal teacher salaries through the Gate City Teachers Association.
Worked with the NAACP and served on the Atlanta Urban League’s first board.
Organized a night school for Black Atlantans.

Worked as bookkeeper, secretary and treasurer of Ivey Brothers Funeral Home, established by her brothers Henry and James in 1912.
Helped operate a family business known for supporting churches, charitable work and families with limited financial means.

row.Institutional Connection and Legacy:

Raised her family with Martin Luther King Sr. and was the mother of Martin Luther King Jr.

row.Name: Flora Ethelwyn Zeto Malekebu
row.College connection: Graduated from Spelman?s high school program in 1915. The college?s Gordon-Zeto Center for Global Education was named in part for her.
row.Institutional Connection and Legacy:
Graduated from Spelman’s high school program in 1915, becoming its first African graduate.
Spelman’s Gordon-Zeto Center for Global Education was named in part for her.
row.Biography:
Came from the Congo to Atlanta as a child with Spelman alumna and missionary Clara A. Howard.
Married physician Daniel Sharpe Malekebu, who had come from Africa with a missionary and later trained at Meharry Medical College.
Worked with her husband in African missions and maintained connections with supporters in the United States.
Served as an assistant at Providence Industrial Mission in Nyasaland.

row.Name: Dinah Watts Pace
row.College connection: Graduated from Atlanta University in 1883 with training in education.
row.Institutional Connection and Legacy:
Graduated from Atlanta University’s Normal Department in June 1883 and began teaching in Covington that summer.
Employed three fellow Atlanta University graduates or former students as teachers at the Reed Home and School.
Taught Bazoline Estelle Usher and recommended her for Atlanta University’s preparatory school. Usher later graduated from the university and became supervisor of education for Black students in Atlanta’s public schools.
row.Biography:
Organized a Sunday school for children in Atlanta’s Summerhill neighborhood after the Civil War. It developed into Pleasant Grove, later Reed Street Baptist Church and today Paradise Missionary Baptist Church.
Alongside her classroom teaching in Covington, visited families and helped care for their children. She began taking orphaned children into her own home.
Founded the Covington Colored Orphans Home in 1890, later known as the Reed Home and Industrial School, providing children with housing, care, and education.
Combined academic instruction with practical and vocational training. The school accepted children without limiting admission to a single religious denomination.
Expanded from caring for a small group of children to operating a school with several buildings and additional teachers.
Continued the work for decades. Paradise Baptist Church’s history credits her with educating about 700 children by the time of her death in 1933.
row.Sources:

row.Name: Bazoline Estelle Usher
row.College connection: Atlanta University alumna.
row.Institutional Connection and Legacy:
Atlanta University: attended its preparatory school, graduated from the college in 1906, and later earned a master’s degree in education.
Spelman College: taught for three years after retiring from Atlanta’s public schools in 1954.
University of Chicago: pursued graduate study.
row.Biography:
Taught in Virginia before returning to Atlanta’s public schools, where she worked as a classroom teacher, assistant principal, and principal.
Served as assistant principal at Booker T. Washington High School and became principal of David T. Howard Grammar School in 1929.
Became supervisor of education for Black students in Atlanta in 1944, then the highest position held by a Black educator in the city’s school system.
Helped establish Girl Scout troops for Black girls in Atlanta in 1943 and recruited Black women to lead the troops, organized as District V.

row.Name: Adrienne McNeil Herndon
row.College connection: Graduated from Atlanta University's Normal Department in 1890 and later taught at the university.
row.Institutional Connection and Legacy:
Graduated from Atlanta University’s Normal Department in 1890 and joined its faculty in 1895.
Introduced Shakespeare into the university’s curriculum and taught elocution.
Directed annual Shakespeare productions during commencement season, involving students in public performances.
Trained student actors in concentration, voice control, movement, and character interpretation, describing her methods in “Shakespeare at Atlanta University” in 1906.
Directed The Merchant of Venice in 1905 and The Taming of the Shrew in 1906. The productions raised money for a proposed university auditorium, chapel, and gymnasium.
row.Biography:
Performed on stages in Boston and New York while pursuing a professional acting career.
Faced discriminatory casting that restricted the roles available to Black actresses.
Studied at the Boston School of Expression and performed a one-woman presentation of Antony and Cleopatra in Boston in 1904.
Took a leading role in planning the Herndon family home near Atlanta University, including spaces intended for university gatherings and theatrical performances.

row.Name: Mattiwilda Dobbs
row.College connection: Graduated from Spelman College in 1946. Returned as artist-in-residence in 1974–1975.
row.Institutional Connection and Legacy:
Began formal voice training at Spelman with Naomi Maise and Willis Laurence James, and sang in the Spelman College Glee Club. Graduated as valedictorian in 1946.
Returned as artist-in-residence for the 1974–1975 academic year, giving recitals and teaching master classes.
Also taught at the University of Texas and Howard University, where she became a professor of voice.
row.Biography:
Won the International Music Competition in Geneva in 1951 and built an international operatic career. In 1953, became the first Black singer to perform at La Scala in Milan.
Made her Metropolitan Opera debut as Gilda in Rigoletto in 1956 and became the first Black woman offered a long-term contract by the company.
Refused to perform for segregated audiences. In 1962, sang at Atlanta Municipal Auditorium after its desegregation, bringing her performances to an integrated audience in her hometown.
Combined performance with the education of younger singers through university teaching, master classes, and recitals. She also served on the Metropolitan Opera’s board and a National Endowment for the Arts recital panel.

row.Name: Irene Carolyn Dobbs Jackson
row.College connection: Graduated as Spelman College’s valedictorian in 1929. Later taught French, Latin, and music in a career spanning several universities.
row.Institutional Connection and Legacy:
Graduated as Spelman’s valedictorian in 1929 and returned to teach French. Also sang in the college’s Glee Club during her student years.
Taught French, Latin, and music during a 50-year educational career that included Spelman, Clark College, Atlanta University, Jackson State, and North Carolina Central University.
Spent the final 19 years of her teaching career as chair of Foreign Languages at North Carolina Central University.
row.Biography:
Pursued advanced study in France at the University of Toulouse, earning a doctorate in French before resuming her teaching in Atlanta.
Challenged the exclusion of Black residents from Atlanta’s main public library by applying for a library card in 1959. Her successful application helped open access to the previously segregated library.
Continued her work as a language scholar and educator across several historically Black institutions, combining classroom teaching with academic leadership.
